**The practical rule.** Classify every candidate covariate as pre-treatment or post-treatment using the causal graph, before running any regression. For the back-door adjustment strategy used here, choose a set of pretreatment covariates that satisfies the criterion; validity is a property of the set jointly, not of each variable separately.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: Choosing among Valid Adjustment Sets

The back-door criterion usually admits several valid sets, and all of them identify the same quantity. A superset of a valid set is not automatically valid: an added variable can open a collider path. Among valid sets, smaller sets reduce positivity and modeling burdens, but they are not uniformly more efficient: a pretreatment variable that predicts the outcome strongly can improve precision, while one that mainly predicts treatment can inflate variance. Graphical sufficiency settles validity; the choice among valid sets is an efficiency question. @sec-w5-lin gives a first instance.
:::

## Estimating the ATE by Outcome Regression {#sec-w5-regression}

Identification is now settled: under the conditions of @thm-ident-ate,
$$\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \E\bigl\{\mu(1, X) - \mu(0, X)\bigr\} = \int \bigl\{\mu(1, x) - \mu(0, x)\bigr\}\, p(x)\, dx .$$
The right side contains only observable quantities, but it is a population quantity. This section turns it into an estimator and studies its sampling properties. Throughout, the data are $N$ i.i.d. observations $(Y_i, T_i, X_i)$ from a superpopulation, $X$ is a set of pretreatment covariates satisfying the back-door criterion, and we write
$$P_N f = \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N f(Y_i, T_i, X_i), \qquad P f = \E\{f(Y, T, X)\}.$$
The letter $N$ is the number of observed units here as in @sec-w5-rct, but the probability model is different: there the units were fixed and the assignment random; here the units are a random sample.

### The Plug-In Principle {#sec-w5-plugin}

The identified functional has three unknowns, and each has a natural sample replacement (@tbl-plugin).

| Unknown | Plug-in replacement | What it costs |
|---|---|---|
| $p(x)$ | The empirical distribution of $X_1, \ldots, X_N$: $\int g(x)\,p(x)\,dx \approx P_N g$ | No model for the distribution of $X$ |
| $\mu(1, \cdot)$ | An estimate $\hat\mu(1, \cdot)$ from the treated units | A model or a smoothing method |
| $\mu(0, \cdot)$ | An estimate $\hat\mu(0, \cdot)$ from the control units | A model or a smoothing method |

: The plug-in principle for the identified functional. {#tbl-plugin}

The plug-in estimator is the difference of two regression estimators,
$$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}} = \hat\mu_{1,\mathrm{reg}} - \hat\mu_{0,\mathrm{reg}}, \qquad \hat\mu_{t,\mathrm{reg}} = \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N \hat\mu(t, X_i),$$ {#eq-or}
where $\hat\mu_{t,\mathrm{reg}}$ is the regression estimator of $\E\{Y(t)\}$. The averaging step needs no model for the covariate distribution; all assumptions of this section concern $\hat\mu$.

### The Discrete Case: Simpson's Paradox and Standardization {#sec-w5-std}

When $X$ is categorical, $\mu(t, x)$ can be estimated by the cell mean $\bar Y_{t,x}$ of $Y$ among units with $T = t$ and $X = x$, and @eq-or becomes the *standardization* estimator
$$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{STD}} = \sum_{x \in \mathcal X}\bigl(\bar Y_{1,x} - \bar Y_{0,x}\bigr)\,\hat p(x), \qquad \hat p(x) = \frac{N_x}{N}.$$ {#eq-std}
This is $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}$ with a *saturated* outcome model, one free parameter per cell, so no functional-form assumption is made. It is also called the *g-formula* [@robins1986new] and *direct standardization*.

::: {#exm-simpson}
## Simpson's Paradox as a Standardization

Return to the vaccination data of Chapter 1 (@sec-w1-simpson): $N = 1{,}000$ people, with $X = 1$ for the elderly. The vaccinated group contains 360 elderly and 60 young people; the unvaccinated group, 40 elderly and 540 young. The risks of illness are $\mu(1, \text{elderly}) = 30\%$, $\mu(0, \text{elderly}) = 50\%$, $\mu(1, \text{young}) = 5\%$, and $\mu(0, \text{young}) = 10\%$, so the vaccine lowers the risk in both strata. Three contrasts weight the strata differently.

- **Pooled.** Each arm uses its own covariate mix, $P(X = 1 \mid T = 1) = 360/420 = 6/7$ and $P(X = 1 \mid T = 0) = 40/580 \approx 0.069$:
$$100\Bigl(\frac{111}{420} - \frac{74}{580}\Bigr) \approx 26.43\% - 12.76\% \approx +13.7 \text{ percentage points}.$$
- **ATE (standardized).** Both arms use $P(X = 1) = 0.40$: $0.4(-20) + 0.6(-5) = -11.0$ percentage points.
- **ATT.** Both arms use $P(X \mid T = 1)$: $\tfrac67(-20) + \tfrac17(-5) \approx -17.9$ percentage points.

The pooled comparison reverses the sign because the vaccinated are mostly elderly, who have a higher baseline risk. The ATT is more negative than the ATE because the treated are concentrated in the stratum with the larger effect. The reversal itself is a fact about conditional proportions; which comparison is causal is a fact about the graph. The standardized answers are causal only under the maintained assumptions: age is a sufficient adjustment set, with positivity and consistency.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Regression Adjustment and Standardization: One Procedure

|  | **Regression adjustment** | **Standardization** |
|---|---|---|
| How $\hat\mu(t, x)$ is estimated | A parametric model or a flexible learner | Cell means |
| Works when $X$ is | Continuous or moderately high-dimensional | Discrete and low-dimensional |
| Main vulnerability | Model misspecification | Sparse or empty cells |
| Averaging step | Predict both conditional means for every unit; average the contrasts | Same |
:::

### The Outcome Model and the Regression Estimator {#sec-w5-outcome-model}

When $X$ is continuous or has many categories, cell means are not available, and $\mu$ is modeled.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## The Three-Step Recipe (Outcome Regression, g-Computation)

Assume $\mu(t, x) = m(t, x; \beta)$ with $m$ known and $\beta$ finite-dimensional.

1. **Fit.** Estimate $\beta$ by least squares (or maximum likelihood) and set $\hat\mu(t, x) = m(t, x; \hat\beta)$.
2. **Predict.** For *every* unit, whatever its observed treatment, compute $\hat\mu(1, X_i)$ and $\hat\mu(0, X_i)$. These are predicted conditional means $\E\{Y(t) \mid X = X_i\}$, not the unit's own potential outcomes, and their difference is not an estimate of the unit-level effect.
3. **Average.** $\hat\mu_{t,\mathrm{reg}} = N^{-1}\sum_i\hat\mu(t, X_i)$ and $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}} = \hat\mu_{1,\mathrm{reg}} - \hat\mu_{0,\mathrm{reg}}$, as in @eq-or.

For the ATT, average the fitted contrasts over the treated units only: $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{ATT}} = N_1^{-1}\sum_{i:\,T_i=1}\{\hat\mu(1, X_i) - \hat\mu(0, X_i)\}$. The variant $N_1^{-1}\sum_{i:\,T_i=1}\{Y_i - \hat\mu(0, X_i)\}$ uses the observed treated outcomes and models $\mu(0, \cdot)$ only, matching the preceding remark on the ATT.
:::

Two linear choices of $m$ are common.

- **Model (a), additive:** $m(t, x; \beta) = \alpha + \tau t + \gamma^\top x$. Then $m(1, x) - m(0, x) = \tau$ for every $x$, and $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is the OLS coefficient on $T$. The model imposes the same conditional average effect at every covariate value, so it forces $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \tau_{\mathrm{ATT}}$; it does not require identical unit-level effects.
- **Model (b), one model per arm:** $m(t, x; \beta) = \alpha_t + \gamma_t^\top x$, fitted separately on each arm. Then $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}} = (\hat\alpha_1 - \hat\alpha_0) + (\hat\gamma_1 - \hat\gamma_0)^\top \bar X$, with $\bar X = N^{-1}\sum_iX_i$.

::: {#prp-centering}
## Model (b): Each Regression Estimator Is an Intercept after Centering

Under model (b), write $\hat\mu(t, x) = \hat a_t + \hat\gamma_t^\top(x - \bar X)$ with $\hat a_t = \hat\alpha_t + \hat\gamma_t^\top\bar X$. Then

1. $\hat\mu_{t,\mathrm{reg}} = \hat a_t$, the intercept of the arm-$t$ regression of $Y$ on $(1, X - \bar X)$, so $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}} = \hat a_1 - \hat a_0$;
2. in the single regression of $Y$ on $\bigl(1,\, T,\, X - \bar X,\, T(X - \bar X)\bigr)$ fitted to all $N$ units, the coefficient on $T$ equals $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}$.
:::

*Proof.* (i) Averaging over all $N$ units, $N^{-1}\sum_i\hat\mu(t, X_i) = \hat a_t + \hat\gamma_t^\top(\bar X - \bar X) = \hat a_t$. (ii) The single regression has a separate intercept and slope for each arm, so its fitted values on arm $t$ are those of the arm-$t$ regression on $(1, X - \bar X)$. Its intercept is $\hat a_0$, and the coefficient on $T$ is $\hat a_1 - \hat a_0$. $\square$

Centering at the arm-specific mean $\bar X_t$ instead of the full-sample mean $\bar X$ would make the intercept equal $\bar Y_t$, and no adjustment would take place. Under model (b) the ATT estimator is $\hat a_1 - \hat a_0 + (\hat\gamma_1 - \hat\gamma_0)^\top(\bar X_1 - \bar X)$, with $\bar X_1$ the treated-arm covariate mean.

### A Worked Example {#sec-w5-worked}

::: {#exm-earnings}
## Earnings and a Binary Covariate

Let $X \in \{0, 1\}$ be a binary covariate and $Y$ earnings in thousands of dollars. The cell means within each arm are:

| $X$ | $N$ (treated) | $\bar Y$ (treated) | $N$ (control) | $\bar Y$ (control) |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0 | 30 | 42 | 70 | 35 |
| 1 | 70 | 58 | 30 | 50 |
| All | 100 | 53.2 | 100 | 39.5 |

The unadjusted difference is $53.2 - 39.5 = 13.7$. But $X = 1$ units, which have higher baseline earnings, make up 70% of the treated and 30% of the controls, so $X$ confounds the comparison. With the cell means as $\hat\mu$, the within-stratum contrasts are $42 - 35 = 7$ for $X = 0$ and $58 - 50 = 8$ for $X = 1$. In the full sample, half the units have $X = 1$, so
$$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}} = 0.5(7) + 0.5(8) = 7.5, \qquad \hat\tau_{\mathrm{ATT}} = 0.3(7) + 0.7(8) = 7.7 .$$
The adjusted estimates are roughly half the unadjusted difference. The ATT is slightly larger because the treated are concentrated in the stratum with the larger contrast.
:::

### The Goal, the Obstacle, and the Nuisance Parameter {#sec-w5-nuisance}

The goal is statistical inference with $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}$: consistency for $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}$, an asymptotic distribution, and a variance estimate, so that a confidence interval can be reported. The obstacle is that $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is not a sample mean. It averages *fitted* values, and the data enter through $\hat\beta$ inside $m$, so the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem do not apply to it directly.

The source of the difficulty is a second parameter. The parameter of interest is $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \E\{\mu(1, X) - \mu(0, X)\}$. The *nuisance parameter* is $\beta$, the coefficient of the outcome model, and more generally the regression function $\mu$ itself. It is not wanted for its own sake, but $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}$ depends on it, so it must be estimated first, and its estimation error propagates into $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}$. The same structure returns in later chapters, with the propensity score (Chapter 6) and with two nuisance functions (Chapters 11 and 12).

For a linear outcome model the propagation can be written exactly. Let
$$\mu(t, x) = z(t, x)^\top\beta_0, \qquad z_d(x) = z(1, x) - z(0, x), \qquad Z_i = z(T_i, X_i),$$
with $z$ known, and let $\hat\beta = (P_NZZ^\top)^{-1}P_NZY$ be the OLS estimator. For model (b), $z(t, x) = (t,\, 1 - t,\, t\,x^\top,\, (1 - t)\,x^\top)^\top$, $\beta = (\alpha_1, \alpha_0, \gamma_1^\top, \gamma_0^\top)^\top$, and $z_d(x) = (1, -1, x^\top, -x^\top)^\top$. For model (a), $z(t, x) = (1, t, x^\top)^\top$ and $z_d = (0, 1, 0^\top)^\top$ is constant. Because $m$ is linear in $\beta$, the average of the predictions is the prediction at the average:
$$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}} = P_N\bigl(z_d^\top\hat\beta\bigr) = (P_Nz_d)^\top\hat\beta, \qquad \tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = (Pz_d)^\top\beta_0 ,$$ {#eq-linearity}
where the second equality uses @thm-ident-ate and the correct specification of the model. For model (b), $P_Nz_d = (1, -1, \bar X^\top, -\bar X^\top)^\top$. The nuisance enters $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}$ through one vector, $\hat\beta$.

### Consistency: Estimation Error and Sampling Error {#sec-w5-consistency}

Subtracting the two displays in @eq-linearity gives an exact decomposition:
$$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}} - \tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \underbrace{(P_Nz_d)^\top(\hat\beta - \beta_0)}_{\text{estimation error}} + \underbrace{(P_N - P)\bigl(z_d^\top\beta_0\bigr)}_{\text{sampling error}} .$$ {#eq-reg-decomp}
The estimation error comes from estimating the nuisance parameter; the sampling error comes from averaging over the sampled covariates instead of their population distribution.

::: {#prp-reg-consistency}
## Consistency of the Regression Estimator

Assume the conditions of @thm-ident-ate, i.i.d. data, a correctly specified linear model $\E(Y \mid T, X) = Z^\top\beta_0$, finite second moments of $Y$ and $Z$, $\E\|z_d(X)\| < \infty$, and a nonsingular $A = \E(ZZ^\top)$. Then $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}} \pto \tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}$.
:::

*Proof.* OLS is a continuous function of the averages $P_NZZ^\top$ and $P_NZY$, which converge to $A$ and $\E(ZY) = A\beta_0$ by the law of large numbers and correct specification; hence $\hat\beta \pto \beta_0$. Since $P_Nz_d \pto Pz_d$, the estimation error tends to zero by Slutsky's theorem. The sampling error is the average of i.i.d. mean-zero terms, so it tends to zero by the law of large numbers. $\square$

The two assumptions have two different jobs. Identification (@thm-ident-ate) makes $\E\{\mu(1, X) - \mu(0, X)\}$ the ATE. The outcome model makes $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}$ consistent for it, because correct specification is what makes OLS converge to the $\beta_0$ that defines $\mu$. Under model (a), $z_d$ is constant, so the sampling error vanishes and $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}} = \hat\tau_{\mathrm{OLS}}$.

### Asymptotic Normality and Variance Estimation {#sec-w5-asymp}

The decomposition @eq-reg-decomp reduces the problem to the asymptotics of the nuisance estimator.

::: {#lem-ols}
## OLS under a Correct Linear Model

Let $Y = Z^\top\beta_0 + \varepsilon$ with $\E(\varepsilon \mid Z) = 0$, i.i.d. data, $\E\|Z\|^4 < \infty$, $\E\varepsilon^4 < \infty$, and $A = \E(ZZ^\top)$ nonsingular; $\mathrm{Var}(\varepsilon \mid Z)$ may depend on $Z$. With $B = \E(\varepsilon^2ZZ^\top)$,
$$\sqrt N(\hat\beta - \beta_0) = A^{-1}\sqrt N\,P_N(Z\varepsilon) + o_p(1) \;\xrightarrow{d}\; N\bigl(0,\, A^{-1}BA^{-1}\bigr).$$
:::

*Proof.* Substituting $Y = Z^\top\beta_0 + \varepsilon$ into $\hat\beta$ gives the exact identity $\hat\beta - \beta_0 = (P_NZZ^\top)^{-1}P_N(Z\varepsilon)$. By the law of large numbers, $(P_NZZ^\top)^{-1} \pto A^{-1}$. The terms $Z_i\varepsilon_i$ are i.i.d. with mean $\E\{Z\,\E(\varepsilon \mid Z)\} = 0$ and variance $B$, so $\sqrt N P_N(Z\varepsilon) \xrightarrow{d} N(0, B)$ by the central limit theorem; Slutsky's theorem completes the proof. $\square$

The matrix $A^{-1}BA^{-1}$ is the *sandwich* variance. It is estimated by $\hat A^{-1}\hat B\hat A^{-1}$ with $\hat A = P_NZZ^\top$, $\hat B = P_N\hat\varepsilon^2ZZ^\top$, and $\hat\varepsilon_i = Y_i - Z_i^\top\hat\beta$. Under homoskedasticity, $B = \sigma^2A$ and it reduces to the classical $\sigma^2A^{-1}$.

::: {#thm-reg-an}
## Asymptotic Normality of the Regression Estimator

Under the conditions of @prp-reg-consistency and @lem-ols, assume also $\E\|z_d(X)\|^2 < \infty$, and let $c = Pz_d$ and
$$\varphi_i = \bigl\{z_d(X_i)^\top\beta_0 - \tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}\bigr\} + c^\top A^{-1}Z_i\varepsilon_i .$$ {#eq-reg-if}
Then $\sqrt N(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}} - \tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}) = \sqrt N\,P_N\varphi + o_p(1) \xrightarrow{d} N\{0, \mathrm{Var}(\varphi)\}$, and
$$\mathrm{Var}(\varphi) = \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}\bigl\{z_d(X)^\top\beta_0\bigr\}}_{\text{sampling error}} + \underbrace{c^\top A^{-1}BA^{-1}c}_{\text{estimation error}} .$$ {#eq-reg-var}
:::

*Proof.* Multiply @eq-reg-decomp by $\sqrt N$. By @lem-ols, $\sqrt N(\hat\beta - \beta_0) = O_p(1)$, and $P_Nz_d = c + o_p(1)$, so the estimation error is $c^\top A^{-1}\sqrt N P_N(Z\varepsilon) + o_p(1)$. Adding the sampling error gives $\sqrt N P_N\varphi + o_p(1)$, and the central limit theorem applies to the i.i.d. mean-zero terms $\varphi_i$, which have finite variance by the moment conditions. For the variance, the correct conditional-mean model gives $\E(\varepsilon \mid T, X) = 0$, and both $z_d(X)$ and $Z$ are functions of $(T, X)$, so the cross term is
$$\E\bigl[\{z_d(X)^\top\beta_0 - \tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}\}\,c^\top A^{-1}Z\, \E(\varepsilon \mid T, X)\bigr] = 0 . \qquad \square$$

The moment condition on $z_d(X)$ is not implied by those on $Z$ for a general $z(t, x)$: $Z$ involves only the received treatment, and a component that matters only under the unreceived treatment can be large where that treatment is rare. For models (a) and (b), $z_d(X)$ is a subvector of $Z$ up to sign, or constant, and the condition is automatic.

The function $\varphi$ is the *influence function* of $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}$: to first order, the estimator behaves like the sample mean of $\varphi_i$. Its two components are the two errors of @eq-reg-decomp, to first order, and they are uncorrelated because the correct model gives $\E(\varepsilon \mid T, X) = 0$. The exact finite-sample terms of @eq-reg-decomp need not be uncorrelated.

**Variance estimation.** With $\hat c = P_Nz_d$ and the plug-in quantities above,
$$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}) = \frac1N\Bigl[P_N\bigl\{z_d(X)^\top\hat\beta - \hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}\bigr\}^2 + \hat c^\top\hat A^{-1}\hat B\hat A^{-1}\hat c\Bigr]$$ {#eq-reg-varhat}
is consistent for $N^{-1}\mathrm{Var}(\varphi)$ by the law of large numbers and continuity, and $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}} \pm 1.96\,\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}$ is an asymptotic 95% confidence interval. An asymptotically equivalent estimator is $N^{-2}\sum_i\hat\varphi_i^2$, with $\hat\varphi_i$ the plug-in influence values. The two are not identical in finite samples: the normal equations do not make the sample cross term between the two components vanish, but it is $o_p(N^{-1})$.

::: {.callout-warning icon=false}
## Two Shortcuts That Miss a Component

The sample variance of the fitted contrasts alone omits the estimation error; under model (a) it is zero. Under model (b), even the sandwich standard error of the $T$ coefficient in the centered interacted regression of @prp-centering omits the sampling error from averaging over a random covariate distribution. Under model (a) the sampling error is zero, and @eq-reg-varhat reduces to the sandwich variance of the $T$ coefficient; the classical OLS standard error is valid under homoskedasticity, and the sandwich also allows heteroskedasticity.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: The Sandwich Formula for a General M-Estimator

OLS is one M-estimator. If $\hat\beta$ solves $P_N\psi(O; \beta) = 0$ and $\beta_0$ solves $P\psi(O; \beta) = 0$, then under regularity conditions $\sqrt N(\hat\beta - \beta_0) = -\dot\Psi^{-1}\sqrt N P_N\psi(O; \beta_0) + o_p(1)$, with $\dot\Psi = \E\{\partial\psi(O; \beta_0)/\partial\beta^\top\}$, and the asymptotic variance is $\dot\Psi^{-1}\E(\psi\psi^\top)\dot\Psi^{-\top}$. Least squares has $\psi = Z(Y - Z^\top\beta)$, $\dot\Psi = -A$, and $\E(\psi\psi^\top) = B$. The extension of @thm-reg-an to an outcome model $m(t, x; \beta)$ fitted by an M-estimator, for example logistic regression, involves two derivatives. Let $\delta(X; \beta) = m(1, X; \beta) - m(0, X; \beta)$ and $c = \E\{\partial_\beta\delta(X; \beta_0)\}$. If $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \E\{\delta(X; \beta_0)\}$ and the usual differentiability and moment conditions hold, the influence function of $P_N\delta(X; \hat\beta)$ is
$$\varphi(O) = \delta(X; \beta_0) - \tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} - c^\top\dot\Psi^{-1}\psi(O; \beta_0),$$
and the asymptotic variance is $\mathrm{Var}\{\varphi(O)\}$. For least squares, $-c^\top\dot\Psi^{-1}\psi = c^\top A^{-1}Z\varepsilon$, recovering @eq-reg-if. The variance splits into two components without a covariance term only under an additional orthogonality condition, for example $\E\{\psi(O; \beta_0) \mid T, X\} = 0$; it should not be asserted for an arbitrary estimating equation.
:::

### What Can Go Wrong {#sec-w5-wrong}

**Misspecification.** If the true $\mu(t, x)$ is nonlinear and a linear model is fitted, OLS converges to the best linear approximation, not to the $\beta_0$ that defines $\mu$, and $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}$ absorbs part of the functional-form error. The bias can have either sign.

**Extrapolation.** Step 2 predicts $\hat\mu(0, X_i)$ for treated units whose $X_i$ may lie outside the support of the controls. There the model, not comparable units, supplies the answer. The overlap condition of Chapter 6 formalizes when extrapolation is unavoidable.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: Consistency beyond a Parametric Model

For a general estimator $\hat\mu_t = \hat\mu(t, \cdot)$, the analogue of @eq-reg-decomp is
$$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}} - \tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = P_N(\hat\mu_1 - \mu_1) - P_N(\hat\mu_0 - \mu_0) + (P_N - P)(\mu_1 - \mu_0).$$
The last term tends to zero by the law of large numbers. The first two tend to zero if $P_N|\hat\mu_t - \mu_t| \pto 0$ for each $t$, an *empirical*-$L_1$ condition. The empirical form matters because $\hat\mu$ is fitted and evaluated on the same observations: convergence in $L_1(P_X)$ alone is not enough. The condition follows from uniform convergence, from $L_1(P_X)$ convergence with suitable Glivenko--Cantelli or stability conditions, or from cross-fitted evaluation. It is sufficient, not necessary: if $\hat\mu_t$ converges to a wrong limit $\mu_t^\ast$, the estimator targets $\E\{\mu_1^\ast(X) - \mu_0^\ast(X)\}$, which can equal $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}$ even when both limits are wrong everywhere. @sec-w5-lin and the lab of @sec-w5-lab show that randomization produces exactly this cancellation for linear working models. In an observational study no design guarantees it.
:::

**Flexible learners and cross-fitting.** A more flexible outcome estimator can reduce approximation bias, at the price of more estimation variability. Cross-fitting separates fitting from evaluation, but alone it guarantees neither consistency nor $\sqrt N$ inference. Chapters 11 and 12 develop estimators whose leading error is less sensitive to errors in the outcome and propensity-score functions.

## Regression Estimation under Complete Randomization {#sec-w5-lin}

@sec-w5-regression justified the regression estimator $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}$ by a *correct* outcome model, with the $N$ units treated as an i.i.d. sample. This section returns to the design-based setting of @sec-w5-rct: the $N$ units form a fixed finite population $\mathcal F_N$, $N_1$ are treated by the CRD, and the only randomness is the assignment. In this setting the difference in means is already exactly unbiased for $\bar\tau_N$ with no model. If we fit the regression anyway, what happens when the linear model is wrong?

The answer, due to @lin2013agnostic, is that the *design*, not the model, justifies $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}$. It is design consistent whether or not the linear model holds, and asymptotically it cannot be less precise than $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{DIM}}$. The proof is the survey-sampling argument for the regression estimator, applied to each arm. @tbl-frameworks places this section beside @sec-w5-regression; it is easy to carry an assumption from one framework into the other by mistake.

| Framework | Target | Source of randomness | Role of the outcome regression |
|---|---|---|---|
| Finite-population CRD (this section) | $\bar\tau_N$ | Assignment | A working approximation used for precision; correct specification is not needed for the design asymptotics |
| I.i.d. observational data (@sec-w5-regression) | $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}$ | Sampling of $(Y, T, X)$ | Correct specification gives the consistency and variance results proved there |
| I.i.d. units followed by the CRD | $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}$ | Sampling and assignment | Inference must account for assignment uncertainty and for variation in the sampled population |

: Three probability frameworks for the regression estimator. {#tbl-frameworks}

::: {#exm-alo}
## Incentives and Services for College Achievement

@angrist2009incentives randomized first-year undergraduates at a Canadian university to support services, financial incentives (awards of \$1,000 to \$5,000 for meeting a target grade), both, or neither. Following @lin2013agnostic [Table 2], we use the men in two of the four arms, with first-year GPA observed: services and incentives ($N_1 = 58$) versus services only ($N_0 = 99$). The contrast is the effect of *adding* incentives when services are offered. The outcome is first-year GPA, and the covariate is high-school GPA, observed for everyone. Randomization makes the two groups comparable on average, but in the realized assignment their high-school GPAs differ a little. Can we use high-school GPA to adjust, and does it help? @sec-w5-lin-example returns to the data.
:::

### Two Regression Estimators and Three Forms {#sec-w5-three-forms}

Let $\mathbf x_i$ be the covariate vector of unit $i$, including an intercept, and assume each arm's design matrix has full column rank. Fit OLS separately in the two arms:
$$\hat{\mathbf B}_1 = \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^N T_i\mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^\top\Bigr)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N T_i\mathbf x_iY_i, \qquad \hat{\mathbf B}_0 = \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^N (1 - T_i)\mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^\top\Bigr)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N (1 - T_i)\mathbf x_iY_i .$$
The estimator of $\bar\tau_N$ is the difference of two regression estimators,
$$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}} = \hat\mu_{1,\mathrm{reg}} - \hat\mu_{0,\mathrm{reg}}, \qquad \hat\mu_{t,\mathrm{reg}} = \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf x_i^\top\hat{\mathbf B}_t = \bar{\mathbf x}^\top\hat{\mathbf B}_t,$$ {#eq-lin-reg}
which is the estimator of @sec-w5-regression under model (b). Write $\mathbf x_i = (1, \mathbf u_i^\top)^\top$, so that $\mathbf u_i$ collects the nonconstant covariates. By @prp-centering, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is also the coefficient on $T$ in the interacted regression of $Y$ on $\bigl(1, T, (\mathbf u - \bar{\mathbf u})^\top, T(\mathbf u - \bar{\mathbf u})^\top\bigr)$; the intercept coordinate is omitted from the centered and interaction terms, which would otherwise contain zero columns. With one covariate, $\mathbf x_i = (1, X_i)^\top$ and $\hat{\mathbf B}_1 = (\hat\alpha_1, \hat b_1)^\top$,
$$\hat\mu_{1,\mathrm{reg}} = \hat\alpha_1 + \bar X\hat b_1 = \hat{\bar Y}_1 + \bigl(\bar X - \hat{\bar X}_1\bigr)\hat b_1,$$
where $\hat{\bar Y}_1$ and $\hat{\bar X}_1$ are treated-arm means. When the treated arm has a higher covariate mean than the population and the slope is positive, the adjustment lowers the estimated mean.

::: {#lem-three-forms}
## Three Forms of the Regression Estimator

Let $\hat e_i = Y_i - \mathbf x_i^\top\hat{\mathbf B}_1$ be the fitted residuals of the treated units. Then
$$\underbrace{\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf x_i^\top\hat{\mathbf B}_1}_{\text{projection form}} = \underbrace{\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf x_i^\top\hat{\mathbf B}_1 + \frac1{N_1}\sum_{i=1}^NT_i\hat e_i}_{\text{projection}\,+\,\text{expansion estimator of the residual mean}} = \underbrace{\hat{\bar Y}_1 + (\bar{\mathbf x} - \hat{\bar{\mathbf x}}_1)^\top\hat{\mathbf B}_1}_{\text{direct}\,+\,\text{augmentation}} .$$ {#eq-three-forms}
:::

*Proof.* The normal equations of the treated-arm fit are $\sum_iT_i\mathbf x_i\hat e_i = \mathbf 0$. The first component of $\mathbf x_i$ is $1$, so $\sum_iT_i\hat e_i = 0$ and the added term is zero. Expanding $\hat e_i$ gives $N_1^{-1}\sum_iT_i\hat e_i = \hat{\bar Y}_1 - \hat{\bar{\mathbf x}}_1^\top\hat{\mathbf B}_1$, which yields the last form. $\square$

The second form, projection plus the expansion (Horvitz--Thompson) estimator of the residual mean, is the *generalized regression* (GREG) estimator of survey sampling. Its residual term vanishes here because the OLS normal equations include an intercept and the expansion weights are constant within the arm. Under unequal-probability sampling, whether the analogous term vanishes depends on how the regression coefficients and the expansion weights are defined; when it does not, it is the term that makes GREG design consistent. The third form reads the estimator as the direct estimator $\hat{\bar Y}_1$ corrected by an augmentation term, the covariate imbalance times the slope.

### The Survey-Sampling Setup and the Oracle Difference Estimator {#sec-w5-oracle}

Let $\mathcal F_N = \{(Y_i(1), Y_i(0), \mathbf x_i) : i = 1, \ldots, N\}$ be fixed. Under the CRD, the treated arm is a simple random sample (SRS) of size $N_1$ without replacement, and the control arm is its complement. Arm 1 is therefore a survey: $Y_i(1)$ is observed on the SRS, $\mathbf x_i$ is known for all $N$ units, and $\bar{\mathbf x} = N^{-1}\sum_i\mathbf x_i$ is a *known population mean*. In survey terms, $\hat\mu_{1,\mathrm{reg}}$ is the regression estimator of $\bar Y(1)$. All expectations below are over the assignment, given $\mathcal F_N$, and no model for $Y_i(t)$ is assumed.

::: {#def-diff}
## Difference Estimator

For a *fixed* vector $\mathbf B$, not estimated from the data, the difference estimator of $\bar Y(1)$ is
$$\hat\mu_{1,\mathrm{diff}}(\mathbf B) = \hat{\bar Y}_1 + (\bar{\mathbf x} - \hat{\bar{\mathbf x}}_1)^\top\mathbf B = \frac1{N_1}\sum_{i=1}^NT_i\bigl\{Y_i(1) - (\mathbf x_i - \bar{\mathbf x})^\top\mathbf B\bigr\}.$$
:::

The difference estimator is an SRS mean of the fixed numbers $u_i = Y_i(1) - (\mathbf x_i - \bar{\mathbf x})^\top\mathbf B$, whose population mean is $\bar Y(1)$. It is therefore exactly design unbiased, with $\mathrm{Var}\{\hat\mu_{1,\mathrm{diff}}(\mathbf B) \mid \mathcal F_N\} = (N_1^{-1} - N^{-1})S_u^2$ by @thm-dim. The family contains the plain mean ($\mathbf B = \mathbf 0$). Within it, $S_u^2$ is the variance of $Y(1)$ around the linear function $(\mathbf x - \bar{\mathbf x})^\top\mathbf B$, which is minimized by the *population* OLS coefficient [@cochran1977sampling]
$$\mathbf B_1 = \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^\top\Bigr)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf x_iY_i(1).$$ {#eq-B1}
The *oracle* difference estimator $\hat\mu_{1,\mathrm{diff}}(\mathbf B_1)$ is the most precise member of the family. It is not available: $\mathbf B_1$ needs every $Y_i(1)$. The regression estimator is the same formula with $\mathbf B_1$ replaced by its treated-arm estimate, $\hat\mu_{1,\mathrm{reg}} = \hat\mu_{1,\mathrm{diff}}(\hat{\mathbf B}_1)$. The oracle is a device for the proof: the next subsection shows that $\hat\mu_{1,\mathrm{reg}}$ is asymptotically equivalent to it, so the design properties of the regression estimator are those of an SRS mean of residuals. Define $\mathbf B_0$ in the same way from the $Y_i(0)$, and the population residuals
$$e_i(t) = Y_i(t) - \mathbf x_i^\top\mathbf B_t, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^Ne_i(t) = 0, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf x_ie_i(t) = \mathbf 0,$$
where the last two identities are the population normal equations.

### Linearization and Design Consistency {#sec-w5-linearization}

Asymptotic statements in the design-based framework refer to a sequence of finite populations with $N \to \infty$.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Regularity Conditions [@lin2013agnostic]

1. The number of covariates is fixed, and $N_1/N \to \rho \in (0, 1)$.
2. $N^{-1}\sum_i\mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^\top$ converges to a nonsingular matrix.
3. The fourth moments of $Y_i(1)$, $Y_i(0)$, and $\mathbf x_i$ are bounded, and their first and second population moments converge.
:::

Complete randomization alone does not give stable OLS inverses or the rates used below; the conditions do. We write $R_N = O_p(a_N)$ if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $M < \infty$ with $P(|R_N| > Ma_N) < \varepsilon$ for all large $N$, and $R_N = o_p(a_N)$ if $R_N/a_N \pto 0$.

::: {#lem-rates}
## Rates for SRS Means

Under the regularity conditions, $\hat{\bar{\mathbf x}}_1 - \bar{\mathbf x} = O_p(N^{-1/2})$ and $\hat{\mathbf B}_1 - \mathbf B_1 = O_p(N^{-1/2})$, and likewise for arm 0.
:::

*Proof.* For one coordinate $x$, the treated-arm mean is an SRS mean, so $\E(\hat{\bar x}_1 \mid \mathcal F_N) = \bar x$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\hat{\bar x}_1 \mid \mathcal F_N) = (N_1^{-1} - N^{-1})S_x^2 \le S_x^2/N_1$. By Chebyshev's inequality,
$$P\bigl(|\hat{\bar x}_1 - \bar x| > MN^{-1/2} \bigm| \mathcal F_N\bigr) \le \frac{N}{N_1}\cdot\frac{S_x^2}{M^2},$$
which is at most $C/M^2$ for large $N$ because $N_1/N \to \rho > 0$ and $S_x^2$ is bounded; choose $M$ with $C/M^2 < \varepsilon$. The same argument applies to every SRS mean of a variable with bounded second moment, in particular to the treated-arm means of $\mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^\top$ and $\mathbf x_iY_i(1)$, whose fourth-moment bounds give bounded variances. $\hat{\mathbf B}_1$ and $\mathbf B_1$ are the same smooth function of these means, evaluated at SRS means and at population means respectively, and the limiting Gram matrix is nonsingular, so $\hat{\mathbf B}_1 - \mathbf B_1 = O_p(N^{-1/2})$. $\square$

::: {#thm-lin}
## Asymptotic Equivalence and Design Consistency

Under the CRD and the regularity conditions, with no model for the potential outcomes,
$$\hat\mu_{1,\mathrm{reg}} = \underbrace{\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf x_i^\top\mathbf B_1 + \frac1{N_1}\sum_{i=1}^NT_i\bigl(Y_i - \mathbf x_i^\top\mathbf B_1\bigr)}_{\hat\mu_{1,\mathrm{diff}}(\mathbf B_1)} + \underbrace{(\bar{\mathbf x} - \hat{\bar{\mathbf x}}_1)^\top(\hat{\mathbf B}_1 - \mathbf B_1)}_{O_p(N^{-1})} ,$$ {#eq-lin-linearization}
and likewise for arm 0. Consequently
$$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}} - \bar\tau_N = \underbrace{\frac1{N_1}\sum_{i=1}^NT_ie_i(1) - \frac1{N_0}\sum_{i=1}^N(1 - T_i)e_i(0)}_{\mathrm{DIME}(e)} + O_p(N^{-1}),$$ {#eq-reg-linearization}
and $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}} \pto \bar\tau_N$ in the sense that $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}} - \bar\tau_N \pto 0$.
:::

*Proof.* By @lem-three-forms, adding the zero term $N_1^{-1}\sum_iT_i(Y_i - \mathbf x_i^\top\hat{\mathbf B}_1)$ to $\hat\mu_{1,\mathrm{reg}}$ changes nothing. Replacing $\hat{\mathbf B}_1$ by $\mathbf B_1$ in both terms and collecting the difference gives @eq-lin-linearization; the remainder is a product of two $O_p(N^{-1/2})$ factors by @lem-rates. The intercept and the population normal equation give $N^{-1}\sum_i\mathbf x_i^\top\mathbf B_1 = \bar Y(1)$, and $Y_i = Y_i(1)$ on the treated arm, so $\hat\mu_{1,\mathrm{diff}}(\mathbf B_1) = \bar Y(1) + N_1^{-1}\sum_iT_ie_i(1)$. Subtracting the arm-0 version gives @eq-reg-linearization. Each $e_i(t)$ is fixed with $\sum_ie_i(t) = 0$, and $\E(T_i \mid \mathcal F_N) = N_1/N$, so $\E\{N_1^{-1}\sum_iT_ie_i(1) \mid \mathcal F_N\} = N^{-1}\sum_ie_i(1) = 0$, and its variance is $(N_1^{-1} - N^{-1})S_{e(1)}^2 = O(N^{-1})$. By Chebyshev's inequality the term tends to zero in probability; the same holds for arm 0. $\square$

We write $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg},\ell} = \bar\tau_N + \mathrm{DIME}(e)$ for the *linearized* estimator. It is the difference of two oracle difference estimators, it is exactly design unbiased, and $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}} - \hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg},\ell} = O_p(N^{-1}) = o_p(N^{-1/2})$, so the two share their first-order distribution. The model appears nowhere in the argument: $\mathbf B_1$ is a population projection, and $Y_i(1)$ need not be linear in $\mathbf x_i$. Randomization justifies the *estimator*, not the model.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: Why the Remainder Vanishes Here and Not in an Observational Study

The same algebra holds in an observational study, with the expansion taken around $\mathbf B_1^\ast = \operatorname{plim}\hat{\mathbf B}_1$:
$$\hat\mu_{1,\mathrm{reg}} = \frac1N\sum_i\mathbf x_i^\top\mathbf B_1^\ast + \frac1{N_1}\sum_iT_i\bigl(Y_i - \mathbf x_i^\top\mathbf B_1^\ast\bigr) + (\bar{\mathbf x} - \hat{\bar{\mathbf x}}_1)^\top(\hat{\mathbf B}_1 - \mathbf B_1^\ast).$$
The difference lies in the two factors of the remainder.

|  | Complete randomization | Observational study (@sec-w5-regression) |
|---|---|---|
| Reference coefficient | $\mathbf B_1$ of @eq-B1, the finite-population projection (it depends on $N$) | $\mathbf B_1^\ast$, the projection under the treated covariate distribution; it equals the population projection when the model is correct, and in some other cases |
| Coefficient estimation error | $\hat{\mathbf B}_1 - \mathbf B_1 = O_p(N^{-1/2})$ | $\hat{\mathbf B}_1 - \mathbf B_1^\ast = O_p(N^{-1/2})$ |
| Covariate imbalance $\bar{\mathbf x} - \hat{\bar{\mathbf x}}_1$ | $O_p(N^{-1/2})$: the treated arm is an SRS | $O_p(1)$: it converges to $\E(\mathbf x) - \E(\mathbf x \mid T = 1)$, which may be nonzero |
| Remainder | $O_p(N^{-1})$: negligible | In general of order $N^{-1/2}$: a first-order coefficient-estimation contribution |
| Leading term | $\bar Y(1)$ plus an SRS mean of fixed residuals: design unbiased, no model | Consistent for $\E\{Y(1)\}$ when the model is correct; otherwise only under additional conditions |

Under complete randomization, the covariate imbalance is $O_p(N^{-1/2})$, so estimating the finite-population regression coefficient affects this expansion only through an $O_p(N^{-1})$ remainder. (If the expansion were taken around the fixed limit $\lim_N\mathbf B_1$ instead, the remainder would in general be only $o_p(N^{-1/2})$, because $\mathbf B_1$ may approach its limit slowly. That still gives first-order equivalence, but not the $O_p(N^{-1})$ rate of @eq-lin-linearization.) In an observational study the covariate imbalance may have a nonzero probability limit, which makes coefficient estimation a first-order contribution. Correct specification of the outcome regression is sufficient for consistency. Without it, consistency requires additional conditions, such as cancellation of the average approximation error, and is not guaranteed by the assignment mechanism.
:::

### Design Variance and Conservative Estimation {#sec-w5-lin-variance}

The linearized estimator is a difference in means of the fixed residuals $e_i(1)$ and $e_i(0)$, so @thm-dim applies with $e(t)$ in place of $Y(t)$.

::: {#prp-lin-var}
## Design Variance of the Regression Estimator

Let $S_{e(t)}^2$ and $S_{e(1)-e(0)}^2$ be the finite-population variances (divisor $N - 1$) of the residuals and of their difference. Then
$$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg},\ell} \mid \mathcal F_N) = \frac{S_{e(1)}^2}{N_1} + \frac{S_{e(0)}^2}{N_0} - \frac{S_{e(1)-e(0)}^2}{N} = \Bigl(\frac1{N_1} - \frac1N\Bigr)S_{e(1)}^2 + \Bigl(\frac1{N_0} - \frac1N\Bigr)S_{e(0)}^2 + \frac2NS_{e(0),e(1)} .$$ {#eq-lin-var}
:::

As in Neyman's theorem, $S_{e(1)-e(0)}^2$ is not identified, because no unit shows both residuals. Omitting its *negative* contribution gives the asymptotically conservative estimator
$$\hat V_{\mathrm{reg}} = \frac{s_{\hat e,1}^2}{N_1} + \frac{s_{\hat e,0}^2}{N_0},$$ {#eq-lin-varhat}
where $s_{\hat e,t}^2$ is the sample variance of the fitted residuals in arm $t$. Dropping the covariance term $2N^{-1}S_{e(0),e(1)}$ of the second form instead would *not* be conservative, because that term can have either sign: if $e_i(1) = e_i(0)$ for every unit, it is positive, and dropping it understates the variance. Under the regularity conditions, the sandwich variance of the $T$ coefficient in the interacted regression also estimates the first-order asymptotic design variance consistently or conservatively, with the same leading $O(N^{-1})$ term as $\hat V_{\mathrm{reg}}$ [@lin2013agnostic]. Equation @eq-lin-var is exact for the linearized estimator; turning the distributional approximation into a statement about the actual finite-sample variance of $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}$ requires moment control of the remainder. The target of this inference is the finite-population $\bar\tau_N$.

### Regression Adjustment Cannot Increase the Asymptotic Variance {#sec-w5-lin-precision}

The residuals $e_i(t)$ have smaller spread than the outcomes when $\mathbf x$ predicts $Y(t)$. The precise statement uses two facts about simple random sampling.

::: {#lem-srs-cov}
## Covariances of SRS Means

For fixed population vectors $u$ and $v$ with population covariance $S_{u,v} = (N - 1)^{-1}\sum_i(u_i - \bar u)(v_i - \bar v)$, let $\hat{\bar u}_t$ denote the arm-$t$ mean of $u$. Under the CRD,
$$\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\bar u}_1, \hat{\bar v}_1 \mid \mathcal F_N) = \Bigl(\frac1{N_1} - \frac1N\Bigr)S_{u,v}, \qquad \mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\bar u}_1, \hat{\bar v}_0 \mid \mathcal F_N) = -\frac1NS_{u,v} .$$
:::

*Proof.* The first identity is the polarization of the variance calculation in the proof of @thm-dim, using the assignment covariances @eq-T-covariances. For the second, $\sum_i(1 - T_i)v_i = \sum_iv_i - \sum_iT_iv_i$, and $\sum_iv_i$ is fixed, so $\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\bar u}_1, \hat{\bar v}_0) = -(N_1/N_0)\,\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\bar u}_1, \hat{\bar v}_1) = -(N_1/N_0)(N_1^{-1} - N^{-1})S_{u,v} = -S_{u,v}/N$. $\square$

::: {#thm-lin-precision}
## No Loss of Precision

Under the CRD,
$$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{DIM}} \mid \mathcal F_N) \;\ge\; \mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg},\ell} \mid \mathcal F_N),$$
an exact inequality for the linearized estimator and hence an asymptotic one for $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}$ under the regularity conditions. Equality holds if and only if the covariates carry no linear information about $(1 - \rho_N)Y(1) + \rho_NY(0)$, with $\rho_N = N_1/N$.
:::

*Proof.* Write $Y_i(t) = g_i(t) + e_i(t)$ with $g_i(t) = \mathbf x_i^\top\mathbf B_t$. Since $\bar e(t) = 0$, $\bar Y(t) = \bar g(t)$, and
$$\hat\tau_{\mathrm{DIM}} - \bar\tau_N = \underbrace{\mathrm{DIME}(e)}_{=\,\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg},\ell} - \bar\tau_N} + \underbrace{\bigl\{\mathrm{DIME}(g) - \bar g(1) + \bar g(0)\bigr\}}_{\text{mean zero}},$$
where $\mathrm{DIME}(g) = N_1^{-1}\sum_iT_ig_i(1) - N_0^{-1}\sum_i(1 - T_i)g_i(0)$. The population normal equations give $\sum_ie_i(t)\mathbf x_i = \mathbf 0$ and $\sum_ie_i(t) = 0$, so $S_{e(t),\,g(s)} = 0$ for all $t, s \in \{0, 1\}$. By @lem-srs-cov, each of the four covariances between an arm mean of $e(t)$ and an arm mean of $g(s)$ is a multiple of $S_{e(t),g(s)}$ and hence zero, so $\mathrm{Cov}\{\mathrm{DIME}(e), \mathrm{DIME}(g) \mid \mathcal F_N\} = 0$ and
$$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{DIM}} \mid \mathcal F_N) = \mathrm{Var}\{\mathrm{DIME}(e) \mid \mathcal F_N\} + \mathrm{Var}\{\mathrm{DIME}(g) \mid \mathcal F_N\}.$$
The second term is nonnegative. By the second form of @eq-neyman-variance with $\rho_N = N_1/N$, it equals $S^2_{(1-\rho_N)g(1) + \rho_Ng(0)}/\{N\rho_N(1 - \rho_N)\}$, which is zero if and only if $\mathbf x^\top\{(1 - \rho_N)\mathbf B_1 + \rho_N\mathbf B_0\}$, the population projection of $(1 - \rho_N)Y(1) + \rho_NY(0)$ on $\mathbf x$, is constant. $\square$

The gain is the design variance of $\mathrm{DIME}(g)$, the part of the outcome explained by $\mathbf x$. Adjustment buys precision, never validity; it is useless when the covariates do not predict the outcomes.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: Finite-Sample Bias

The difference in means is exactly design unbiased. The fitted regression estimator is not generally exactly unbiased, although it can be in special populations, for example when the potential outcomes are exactly linear in the included covariates. @thm-lin gives an $O_p(N^{-1})$ remainder, so coefficient estimation has a second-order effect on the stochastic expansion. An $O_p$ statement controls typical size, not expectation: rare, nearly singular arm-wise fits barely affect convergence in probability but can affect the mean. With additional moment conditions that control the expectation of the remainder, the bias is $O(N^{-1})$, while the standard error is of order $N^{-1/2}$, so the bias is then negligible in large experiments. In small experiments, or with many covariates relative to $N_1$ and $N_0$, the bias and the instability of the arm-wise OLS fits can matter, and the unadjusted estimate should be reported alongside the adjusted one.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: Finite-Population and Superpopulation Inference

If the $N$ units are themselves an i.i.d. sample, phase one draws $\mathcal F_N$ and phase two the arms. Since $\E(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg},\ell} \mid \mathcal F_N) = \bar\tau_N$,
$$\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg},\ell}) = \mathrm{Var}(\bar\tau_N) + \E\bigl\{\mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg},\ell} \mid \mathcal F_N)\bigr\}, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\bar\tau_N) = \frac1N\mathrm{Var}\{Y(1) - Y(0)\}.$$
Let $\mathbf b_t$ be the superpopulation projection coefficients and $r(t) = Y(t) - \mathbf x^\top\mathbf b_t$. Projection orthogonality gives $N\,\mathrm{Var}(\bar\tau_N) = \mathrm{Var}\{\mathbf x^\top(\mathbf b_1 - \mathbf b_0)\} + \mathrm{Var}\{r(1) - r(0)\}$. The sandwich variance already omits the negative term $-\mathrm{Var}\{r(1) - r(0)\}$ of the design variance, so for the superpopulation ATE it lacks only the variation of the fitted contrast, the sampling error of @sec-w5-regression:
$$\hat V_{\mathrm{super}} = \hat V_{\mathrm{sandwich}} + \frac1{N^2}\sum_{i=1}^N\bigl\{\mathbf x_i^\top(\hat{\mathbf B}_1 - \hat{\mathbf B}_0) - \hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}\bigr\}^2 ,$$
a large-sample estimator under i.i.d. sampling of units and complete randomization. Adding all of $\mathrm{Var}(\bar\tau_N)$ to the sandwich would count the residual-effect variance twice. A check: if $Y_i(0) = 0$ and $Y_i(1) = X_i$, then $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}} = \bar X = \bar\tau_N$ exactly and the design variance is zero, which is correct for $\bar\tau_N$; but estimating $\E(X)$ from a sample still has variance $\mathrm{Var}(X)/N$, which is the added term. Inference for $\bar\tau_N$ conditions on the enrolled units; inference for $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}$ also accounts for sampling them.
:::

### The Survey-Sampling Precedent and the Example Revisited {#sec-w5-lin-example}

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Remark: Precedence in Survey Sampling

A completely randomized experiment is simple random sampling without replacement from the finite population of potential outcomes, so the results of this section have survey-sampling ancestors. @isaki1982survey established the design consistency of the regression estimator under general probability designs, even when the assisting model is misspecified. @deville1992calibration showed that calibration estimators share this property, with the generalized regression estimator as the case of a quadratic distance and linear calibration weights; @sec-w5-calibration develops this view. @lin2013agnostic adapted the regression estimator to the Neyman--Rubin model: the fully interacted specification cannot hurt asymptotic precision relative to $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{DIM}}$, and the sandwich variance is asymptotically valid or conservative under randomization.
:::

::: {#exm-alo2}
## Incentives and Services, Continued

For the 157 men of @exm-alo, @lin2013agnostic [Table 2] reports:

| Estimator | Estimate | Standard error |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| Difference in means $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{DIM}}$ | $-0.036$ | $0.158$ |
| Regression estimator $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}$ | $-0.081$ | $0.146$ |

The standard errors are uncorrected sandwich standard errors. Both estimators target $\bar\tau_N$, the effect for these 157 men of offering incentives in addition to services. The estimated standard error falls from 0.158 to 0.146 because the regression estimator's variance uses residual variances; a smaller estimated standard error in one data set is consistent with, but does not by itself prove, a smaller true variance. The gain is small because high-school GPA predicts first-year GPA only weakly. The two estimates differ by 0.045, well within one standard error: the adjustment corrects a small chance imbalance in high-school GPA.
:::

## Calibration Weighting {#sec-w5-calibration}

@sec-w5-lin studied $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}}$ through its coefficients $\hat{\mathbf B}_t$. This section studies the same estimator through its *weights*. Each arm's linear regression estimator, fitted by least squares with an intercept, is a weighted mean of the outcomes in its arm, and the weights have two properties: they reproduce the full-sample covariate mean exactly, and among all weights that do so they are the closest to uniform. This is the calibration view of survey sampling [@deville1992calibration]. It explains what regression adjustment does to the covariates, and it is the bridge to stratification (@sec-w5-stratification) and to propensity-score weighting (Chapter 6).

The setting is that of @sec-w5-lin: $\mathbf x_i$ includes an intercept, each arm's design matrix has full column rank, and each weight vector contains only the units of its own arm. We treat arm 1; arm 0 is identical. Write
$$\hat{\mathbf M}_1 = \sum_{i=1}^NT_i\mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^\top, \qquad \hat{\bar{\mathbf x}}_1 = \frac1{N_1}\sum_{i=1}^NT_i\mathbf x_i, \qquad \bar{\mathbf x} = \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbf x_i .$$

### The Regression Estimator as a Weighted Sum {#sec-w5-cal-weights}

Substituting $\hat{\mathbf B}_1 = \hat{\mathbf M}_1^{-1}\sum_iT_i\mathbf x_iY_i$ into $\hat\mu_{1,\mathrm{reg}} = \bar{\mathbf x}^\top\hat{\mathbf B}_1$ gives a linear function of the treated outcomes,
$$\hat\mu_{1,\mathrm{reg}} = \sum_{i=1}^NT_i\,\omega_{1i}Y_i, \qquad \omega_{1i} = \bar{\mathbf x}^\top\hat{\mathbf M}_1^{-1}\mathbf x_i ,$$ {#eq-reg-weights}
and likewise $\hat\mu_{0,\mathrm{reg}} = \sum_i(1 - T_i)\,\omega_{0i}Y_i$ with $\omega_{0i} = \bar{\mathbf x}^\top\{\sum_j(1 - T_j)\mathbf x_j\mathbf x_j^\top\}^{-1}\mathbf x_i$. The weights depend on $\mathbf x$ and $T$ only, not on $Y$, so they can be computed and inspected before any outcome is seen. With $\mathbf x_i = 1$ alone, they are $1/N_1$ and $1/N_0$, and $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{reg}} = \hat\tau_{\mathrm{DIM}}$.

::: {#prp-cal-constraint}
## The Regression Weights Satisfy the Calibration Constraint

$$\sum_{i=1}^NT_i\,\omega_{1i}\mathbf x_i = \bar{\mathbf x}, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^N(1 - T_i)\,\omega_{0i}\mathbf x_i = \bar{\mathbf x}.$$ {#eq-cal-constraint}
:::

*Proof.* $\sum_iT_i\omega_{1i}\mathbf x_i = \sum_iT_i\mathbf x_i\mathbf x_i^\top\hat{\mathbf M}_1^{-1}\bar{\mathbf x} = \hat{\mathbf M}_1\hat{\mathbf M}_1^{-1}\bar{\mathbf x} = \bar{\mathbf x}$; the control arm is the same. $\square$

Each weighted arm reproduces the full-sample covariate mean exactly. The intercept is one of the covariates, so the weights sum to one. Condition @eq-cal-constraint is called the *covariate-balancing* or *calibration* constraint. Balance of these means does not by itself establish exchangeability: it concerns only the covariate functions included in $\mathbf x$. Many weight vectors satisfy @eq-cal-constraint when $N_1 > p$. The rest of this section asks which one the regression estimator uses, and why.

### Which Weights? A Working Model {#sec-w5-cal-model}

Consider all weighted estimators $\hat\mu_{\boldsymbol\omega} = \sum_iT_i\omega_iY_i$ of $\bar Y(1)$ with normalized weights, $\sum_iT_i\omega_i = 1$; the plain mean has $\omega_i = 1/N_1$. To compare them, adopt the working model
$$Y_i(1) = \mathbf x_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \E(\boldsymbol\varepsilon \mid \mathbf X, \mathbf T) = \mathbf 0, \qquad \mathrm{Var}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon \mid \mathbf X, \mathbf T) = \sigma^2\mathbf I_N ,$$
and define the *calibration residual* $\mathbf h(\boldsymbol\omega) = \bar{\mathbf x} - \sum_iT_i\omega_i\mathbf x_i$, the target minus the achieved covariate mean. For fixed weights,
$$\hat\mu_{\boldsymbol\omega} - \bar Y(1) = -\mathbf h(\boldsymbol\omega)^\top\boldsymbol\beta + \sum_{i=1}^N\Bigl(T_i\omega_i - \frac1N\Bigr)\varepsilon_i ,$$
because the target $\bar Y(1)$ contains the same errors as the estimator. Hence, for normalized weights,
$$\mathrm{MSE}\bigl\{\hat\mu_{\boldsymbol\omega} - \bar Y(1) \mid \mathbf X, \mathbf T\bigr\} = \bigl\{\mathbf h(\boldsymbol\omega)^\top\boldsymbol\beta\bigr\}^2 + \sigma^2\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^NT_i\omega_i^2 - \frac1N\Bigr),$$ {#eq-cal-mse}
since $\sum_i(T_i\omega_i - N^{-1})^2 = \sum_iT_i\omega_i^2 - 2N^{-1}\sum_iT_i\omega_i + N^{-1}$. The model supplies the three ingredients of the optimization.

- **The constraint.** $\boldsymbol\beta$ is unknown. The estimator is model-unbiased for *every* $\boldsymbol\beta$ if and only if $\mathbf h(\boldsymbol\omega) = \mathbf 0$: the weighted covariate mean must equal the known $\bar{\mathbf x}$.
- **The distance.** With the bias removed, minimizing the MSE means minimizing $\sum_iT_i\omega_i^2$.
- **The anchor.** On the normalized set, $\sum_iT_i\omega_i^2 = \sum_iT_i(\omega_i - 1/N_1)^2 + 1/N_1$, so the criterion is the Euclidean distance to the *anchor*, the initial weights $1/N_1$.

Only the *form* of the model is used; $\boldsymbol\beta$ is never estimated. The model motivates the criterion; the identity between calibration and OLS in the next subsection does not need it to be true, and the design-based results of @sec-w5-lin do not use it at all.

### $L_2$ Calibration and the Lagrange Multiplier Method {#sec-w5-cal-lagrange}

The calibration problem for arm 1 is
$$\min_{\boldsymbol\omega}\; D(\boldsymbol\omega) = \frac12\sum_{i=1}^NT_i\Bigl(\omega_i - \frac1{N_1}\Bigr)^2 \quad\text{subject to}\quad \mathbf h(\boldsymbol\omega) = \bar{\mathbf x} - \sum_{i=1}^NT_i\omega_i\mathbf x_i = \mathbf 0,$$ {#eq-cal-problem}
with Lagrangian $\mathcal L(\boldsymbol\omega, \boldsymbol\lambda) = D(\boldsymbol\omega) + \boldsymbol\lambda^\top\mathbf h(\boldsymbol\omega)$ and multiplier $\boldsymbol\lambda \in \mathbb R^p$. The multiplier method turns a problem in $N_1$ unknowns into one in $p$ unknowns.

1. **Minimize in $\boldsymbol\omega$ for fixed $\boldsymbol\lambda$.** Setting $\partial\mathcal L/\partial\omega_i = 0$ gives, unit by unit, the *linear weight form*
$$\omega_i^\star(\boldsymbol\lambda) = \frac1{N_1} + \boldsymbol\lambda^\top\mathbf x_i :$$
the anchor plus a linear function of $\mathbf x_i$, with the same $p$ coefficients for every unit.
2. **Maximize the dual.** Substituting, $D(\boldsymbol\omega^\star) = \tfrac12\boldsymbol\lambda^\top\hat{\mathbf M}_1\boldsymbol\lambda$ and $\mathbf h(\boldsymbol\omega^\star) = \bar{\mathbf x} - \hat{\bar{\mathbf x}}_1 - \hat{\mathbf M}_1\boldsymbol\lambda$, so the dual function is the concave quadratic
$$\ell(\boldsymbol\lambda) = \mathcal L\{\boldsymbol\omega^\star(\boldsymbol\lambda), \boldsymbol\lambda\} = \boldsymbol\lambda^\top(\bar{\mathbf x} - \hat{\bar{\mathbf x}}_1) - \frac12\boldsymbol\lambda^\top\hat{\mathbf M}_1\boldsymbol\lambda ,$$
whose gradient is the calibration residual $\mathbf h\{\boldsymbol\omega^\star(\boldsymbol\lambda)\}$.
3. **Return.** $\nabla\ell = \mathbf 0$ gives $\hat{\boldsymbol\lambda} = \hat{\mathbf M}_1^{-1}(\bar{\mathbf x} - \hat{\bar{\mathbf x}}_1)$ and the *regression weights*
$$\hat\omega_i = \frac1{N_1} + (\bar{\mathbf x} - \hat{\bar{\mathbf x}}_1)^\top\hat{\mathbf M}_1^{-1}\mathbf x_i = \bar{\mathbf x}^\top\hat{\mathbf M}_1^{-1}\mathbf x_i .$$ {#eq-cal-solution}
The second form holds because the first column of $\hat{\mathbf M}_1$ is $\sum_iT_i\mathbf x_i = N_1\hat{\bar{\mathbf x}}_1$, so $\hat{\mathbf M}_1^{-1}\hat{\bar{\mathbf x}}_1 = \mathbf e_1/N_1$ and $\hat{\bar{\mathbf x}}_1^\top\hat{\mathbf M}_1^{-1}\mathbf x_i = 1/N_1$.

That the two steps return the solution of @eq-cal-problem is proved in @sec-w5-kkt.

::: {#thm-cal-reg}
## Calibration Equals Regression [@fuller1975regression; @deville1992calibration]

The solution of @eq-cal-problem is $\hat\omega_i = \omega_{1i}$ of @eq-reg-weights, and for *every* outcome variable $Y$,
$$\sum_{i=1}^NT_i\,\hat\omega_iY_i = \bar{\mathbf x}^\top\hat{\mathbf M}_1^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^NT_i\mathbf x_iY_i = \bar{\mathbf x}^\top\hat{\mathbf B}_1 = \hat\mu_{1,\mathrm{reg}} .$$
:::

The identity is exact, not asymptotic. The $N_1$-dimensional weight problem and the $p$-dimensional least-squares problem compute the same number. The weights do not depend on $Y$, and the coefficient does: calibration separates the work on $\mathbf x$, done once, from the work on $Y$, done for each outcome. In an experiment with many outcomes, one set of weights gives the regression estimator for each, and the design consistency of @sec-w5-lin carries over to the weighted form. Nothing in the problem prevents $\hat\omega_i < 0$.

### KKT Conditions and Strong Duality {#sec-w5-kkt}

The multiplier method is an instance of a general characterization. Write $n = N_1$ for the size of arm 1, let $\mathbf X_1$ be the $n \times p$ matrix of treated covariate rows, and consider the calibration set
$$\mathcal C_\omega = \{\boldsymbol\omega \in \mathbb R^n : \mathbf X_1^\top\boldsymbol\omega = \bar{\mathbf x}\}.$$
Two subspaces of $\mathbb R^n$ organize the argument:
$$\mathrm{Col}(\mathbf X_1) = \{\mathbf X_1\mathbf a : \mathbf a \in \mathbb R^p\}, \qquad \mathrm{Ker}(\mathbf X_1^\top) = \{\mathbf k \in \mathbb R^n : \mathbf X_1^\top\mathbf k = \mathbf 0\}.$$
$\mathrm{Ker}(\mathbf X_1^\top)$, the null space of $\mathbf X_1^\top$, contains the directions that leave every weighted $\mathbf x$-mean unchanged. $\mathrm{Col}(\mathbf X_1)$ contains the vectors whose $i$th entry is a linear function $\mathbf x_i^\top\mathbf a$ of the covariates.

::: {#lem-ftla}
## Fundamental Theorem of Linear Algebra

$\mathrm{Ker}(\mathbf X_1^\top) = \mathrm{Col}(\mathbf X_1)^\perp$, so $\mathbb R^n = \mathrm{Col}(\mathbf X_1) \oplus \mathrm{Ker}(\mathbf X_1^\top)$ with the two subspaces orthogonal.
:::

*Proof.* $\mathbf k \in \mathrm{Ker}(\mathbf X_1^\top)$ if and only if $\mathbf k^\top\mathbf X_1\mathbf a = (\mathbf X_1^\top\mathbf k)^\top\mathbf a = 0$ for every $\mathbf a$, that is, if and only if $\mathbf k \perp \mathrm{Col}(\mathbf X_1)$. Every subspace $\mathcal S$ of $\mathbb R^n$ gives $\mathbb R^n = \mathcal S \oplus \mathcal S^\perp$. $\square$

::: {#prp-kkt}
## KKT Conditions for Calibration

Let $D : \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R$ be convex and differentiable, and let $\mathcal C_\omega$ be nonempty. Then $\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}$ minimizes $D$ over $\mathcal C_\omega$ if and only if, for some $\hat{\boldsymbol\lambda} \in \mathbb R^p$,

(i) *feasibility*: $\mathbf X_1^\top\hat{\boldsymbol\omega} = \bar{\mathbf x}$;

(ii) *stationarity*: $\nabla D(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}) = \mathbf X_1\hat{\boldsymbol\lambda}$, that is, $\partial D(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega})/\partial\omega_i = \hat{\boldsymbol\lambda}^\top\mathbf x_i$ for every treated unit.

If $D$ is strictly convex, the minimizer is unique; if $\mathbf X_1$ has full column rank, the multiplier is unique.
:::

*Proof.* *Feasible directions.* For $\hat{\boldsymbol\omega} \in \mathcal C_\omega$, the line $\hat{\boldsymbol\omega} + t\mathbf k$ stays in $\mathcal C_\omega$ for all $t \in \mathbb R$ if and only if $\mathbf X_1^\top\mathbf k = \mathbf 0$. The feasible directions are exactly $\mathrm{Ker}(\mathbf X_1^\top)$, each in both senses.

*Necessity.* Let $\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}$ minimize $D$ over $\mathcal C_\omega$ and let $\mathbf k \in \mathrm{Ker}(\mathbf X_1^\top)$. The function $g(t) = D(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega} + t\mathbf k)$ is differentiable and minimized at $t = 0$ over all of $\mathbb R$, so $0 = g'(0) = \nabla D(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega})^\top\mathbf k$. This holds for every $\mathbf k \in \mathrm{Ker}(\mathbf X_1^\top)$, so $\nabla D(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}) \in \mathrm{Ker}(\mathbf X_1^\top)^\perp = \mathrm{Col}(\mathbf X_1)$ by @lem-ftla.

*Sufficiency.* Let $\hat{\boldsymbol\omega} \in \mathcal C_\omega$ satisfy (ii), and let $\boldsymbol\omega \in \mathcal C_\omega$. Then $\boldsymbol\omega - \hat{\boldsymbol\omega} \in \mathrm{Ker}(\mathbf X_1^\top)$ and $\nabla D(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}) \in \mathrm{Col}(\mathbf X_1)$, so $\nabla D(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega})^\top(\boldsymbol\omega - \hat{\boldsymbol\omega}) = 0$. Convexity gives $D(\boldsymbol\omega) \ge D(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}) + \nabla D(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega})^\top(\boldsymbol\omega - \hat{\boldsymbol\omega}) = D(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega})$.

*Uniqueness.* If $D$ is strictly convex, two minimizers would give a strictly smaller value at their midpoint, which is feasible. If $\mathbf X_1$ has full column rank, $\mathbf X_1\hat{\boldsymbol\lambda} = \mathbf X_1\hat{\boldsymbol\lambda}'$ implies $\hat{\boldsymbol\lambda} = \hat{\boldsymbol\lambda}'$. $\square$

With equality constraints only, the KKT (Karush--Kuhn--Tucker) conditions are (i) and (ii); together they say $\nabla\mathcal L(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}, \hat{\boldsymbol\lambda}) = \mathbf 0$, in $\boldsymbol\omega$ (stationarity) and in $\boldsymbol\lambda$ (feasibility, $\nabla_{\boldsymbol\lambda}\mathcal L = \mathbf h$). For the Euclidean distance, $\nabla D(\boldsymbol\omega) = \boldsymbol\omega - \boldsymbol\omega^{(0)}$ with anchor $\boldsymbol\omega^{(0)} = n^{-1}\mathbf 1$, and stationarity is the linear weight form $\boldsymbol\omega = \boldsymbol\omega^{(0)} + \mathbf X_1\boldsymbol\lambda$ of @sec-w5-cal-lagrange. For a general $D$ it is the *gradient*, not the weights, that is linear in $\mathbf x_i$; a nonlinear $\nabla D$ gives nonlinear weights.

::: {#prp-duality}
## Strong Duality

Assume $D$ is convex and differentiable on $\mathbb R^n$, the constraints are affine, and the primal problem has a minimizer $\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}$. With $\ell(\boldsymbol\lambda) = \inf_{\boldsymbol\omega}\mathcal L(\boldsymbol\omega, \boldsymbol\lambda)$,
$$\max_{\boldsymbol\lambda}\ell(\boldsymbol\lambda) = \ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\lambda}) = D(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}) = \min_{\boldsymbol\omega}\sup_{\boldsymbol\lambda}\mathcal L(\boldsymbol\omega, \boldsymbol\lambda),$$
with $\hat{\boldsymbol\lambda}$ the multiplier of @prp-kkt.
:::

*Proof.* By @prp-kkt, $\nabla D(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}) = \mathbf X_1\hat{\boldsymbol\lambda}$, so $\nabla_{\boldsymbol\omega}\mathcal L(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}, \hat{\boldsymbol\lambda}) = \mathbf 0$. The function $\mathcal L(\cdot, \hat{\boldsymbol\lambda}) = D + \hat{\boldsymbol\lambda}^\top\mathbf h$ is convex, so its stationary point $\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}$ is its global minimizer: step 1 of the multiplier method returns $\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}$ at $\hat{\boldsymbol\lambda}$. Since $\mathbf h(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}) = \mathbf 0$, $\ell(\hat{\boldsymbol\lambda}) = \mathcal L(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}, \hat{\boldsymbol\lambda}) = D(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega})$. For any $\boldsymbol\lambda$, weak duality gives $\ell(\boldsymbol\lambda) \le \mathcal L(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega}, \boldsymbol\lambda) = D(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega})$, so $\hat{\boldsymbol\lambda}$ maximizes $\ell$. Finally, $\sup_{\boldsymbol\lambda}\mathcal L(\boldsymbol\omega, \boldsymbol\lambda)$ equals $D(\boldsymbol\omega)$ on $\mathcal C_\omega$ and $+\infty$ off it, so its minimum is $D(\hat{\boldsymbol\omega})$. $\square$

Strong duality justifies steps 2 and 3 of the multiplier method: maximizing the $p$-dimensional dual returns the multiplier of the primal solution, and the linear weight form at that multiplier is the calibrated weight vector.

### Geometry: Orthogonal Projection {#sec-w5-cal-geometry}

For the Euclidean distance the solution has a geometric reading. $\mathcal C_\omega$ is an affine set, $\mathcal C_\omega = \boldsymbol\omega_1 + \mathrm{Ker}(\mathbf X_1^\top)$ for any $\boldsymbol\omega_1 \in \mathcal C_\omega$, and the level sets of $D(\boldsymbol\omega) = \tfrac12\|\boldsymbol\omega - \boldsymbol\omega^{(0)}\|^2$ are spheres around the anchor. Growing the spheres until one touches $\mathcal C_\omega$ gives the solution. At the touching point, moving along $\mathcal C_\omega$ cannot lower $D$ to first order, so $\hat{\boldsymbol\omega} - \boldsymbol\omega^{(0)} \perp \mathrm{Ker}(\mathbf X_1^\top)$, that is, $\hat{\boldsymbol\omega} - \boldsymbol\omega^{(0)} \in \mathrm{Col}(\mathbf X_1)$: the linear weight form, read as a picture.
